label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
# One Assignment, Except Not Really

Jess texted me last night and said, basically, “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.” Then half the group chat agreed with her.

I get it. I really do. And rather than answer in fifteen increasingly defensive texts, I’m going to explain this once, properly. Jess, this is mostly for you, but it isn’t an argument. I’m not angry at you. You weren’t telling me history doesn’t matter. You were telling me you don’t want me to get hurt.

Also, you know me. We met student teaching at the same school in 2012. You watched me become a teacher before I had any idea what I was doing. You left teaching in 2019 and now do HR at a biotech in Cambridge, which means you probably understand better than I do how an institution can make someone’s life difficult without ever using the word *fired*.

So here’s the assignment.

I teach two sections of junior-year U.S. History II at Cobb Street High. For the past four years, I’ve had students interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston busing and school desegregation in 1974–76. They make a ten-minute recording and write a two-page reflection. We talk beforehand about asking open questions, listening without interrupting, and understanding that memory is evidence, but not the same thing as a transcript.

Until now, no one has complained.

In 2023, D. interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family. Not her children, not her grandchildren. D. came back with this recording of his grandmother describing something she had kept to herself for almost fifty years, and he played forty seconds of it for the class.

When he stopped the recording, nobody said anything. I don’t mean a respectful little classroom pause. I mean nobody moved or spoke for what felt like a full minute. Eventually I realized they were waiting for one another, or maybe for me, and I had nothing useful to add either.

Then last year, a girl interviewed someone in her family and found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. There was no beautiful silence afterward, no feeling that I had engineered some perfect educational moment. We talked after class twice. She was trying to reconcile someone she knew and loved with something she could barely believe he had done.

Her reflection was the best thing I read all year. Not because she arrived at a clean answer, and certainly not because she had been made to suffer for my curriculum. It was the best because it was honest and unsettled. She had stopped treating history as something that happened to strangers.

Both of those experiences are true. I don’t get to keep only the grandmother story and pretend the other one doesn’t complicate things.

The parent’s email went to Dr. Halvorsen and cc’d a school committee member. It said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” Dr. Halvorsen would like me to quietly drop it. My meeting with Halvorsen and the parent is Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

My first reaction was defensive, as you’d expect. Four years. No complaints. Actual family history. Students doing actual historical work. Then I sat with the phrase about judging grandparents, because I don’t think it’s ridiculous.

I’m not going to invent a sinister motive for this parent. My working assumption is that she’s objecting to something she thinks could hurt her kid or complicate her family, not auditioning to be the villain in my blog post. And she has a point about pressure.

Any time you send a teenager home with a recorder and a question about a painful part of the past, you are sending school into a place where school doesn’t automatically belong. Even with the neighborhood option, a student can hear *family or neighborhood* and conclude that the family interview is the real assignment, the impressive one, the one I secretly want.

I don’t want a kid weighing a grade against a conversation they aren’t ready to have. Oral history shouldn’t become a contest over whose family has the most dramatic story. It definitely shouldn’t require a sixteen-year-old to put a grandparent on trial for my benefit.

So I’m changing that part.

My plan is to keep the project and add a genuine alternate option. A student can interview a librarian or archivist instead, or use recorded interviews from previous years, with permission. Same historical work, same expectations, same reflection, same credit. No student will be required to interview a relative, and no student will have to explain to me why they’ve chosen the alternative. That isn’t a lesser track or a favor. It’s another way into the assignment.

That change feels right to me. Dropping the whole project doesn’t.

This is the history of the city my students live in. Not an inset about the city. Not an optional local-color unit if we have a free week in May. The desegregation crisis shaped their neighborhoods, their schools, their families, and, in some cases, decisions their families made without ever calling them political decisions.

The textbook gives Boston busing one paragraph.

One paragraph. And I am supposed to believe the responsible response to “this may reopen wounds” is to return quietly to the paragraph.

I don’t think every wound needs to be poked by a junior with a recording app. I also don’t think silence is neutral. Oral history lets students encounter people who were there, while also learning that no single person’s memory contains the whole event. They have to listen closely, compare accounts, notice what someone avoids, and resist turning a complicated person into either a hero or a villain. Those aren’t decorative skills. That’s history.

Do I think the students most resistant to this material sometimes have the most to gain from encountering it? Yes. I do. But “would benefit” isn’t a permission slip. Discomfort isn’t automatically educational; sometimes it just means a kid has been put in a bad position. I don’t get to force anyone into an intimate family conversation because I have decided it would be good for them. That’s the line.

There’s a difference between teaching difficult history carefully and making a student personally absorb the difficulty so I can feel good about the lesson.

And now the part Jess is actually worried about.

Yes, I could get burned. I’ve been tenured since 2021, which matters, and I’m not going to pretend I have no protection. But tenure does not make Dr. Halvorsen stop controlling my schedule or who gets AP sections. There are plenty of ways for a job to become smaller and worse without anyone formally taking it away. Jess, you absolutely do not need that explained to you.

I understand why a principal wants this to disappear. An email to the principal is one thing; an email with a school committee member copied has a different temperature. Quiet is easier. A replacement worksheet doesn’t generate meetings.

But I don’t want to change the project only because someone complained to the right people. I want to change it because part of the concern is legitimate, and then be able to explain why the rest is worth keeping.

I’m not going into Thursday looking for a fight with the parent. I’m going to listen to her. I’m going to explain the alternate option and make clear that no child has to go home and cross-examine a grandparent. I’m also going to explain what happened when D. pressed play, and what happened for the student whose discovery was much harder to carry.

I’m a little scared. Not in an inspiring way. I don’t feel brave about this. I would very much like everyone at the meeting to be reasonable, for Thursday afternoon to end uneventfully, and for me to keep the schedule and classes I like. I have no interest in turning myself into evidence of my own principles.

But I also don’t want to teach my students that history becomes optional whenever it enters the room and clears its throat.

Jess, you don’t have to agree with me. You were probably right about the risk, and you were definitely right that I should stop and think before turning this into a referendum on my entire career. I hear the part underneath your text: *I know you. Please don’t make yourself bleed for something just because you can.*

I’m not trying to bleed. I’m trying to fix the part that could put too much pressure on a kid, and not abandon the part that teaches them something true about where they live.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting. If it goes badly, you get exactly one “I told you so,” delivered gently. If it goes well, I’m still going to want to hear what you think of the revised assignment.

Either way, I know you’ll answer.
